title: Israel's Gods: The Canaanite Background
description: El, Baal, Asherah, a god from the south, and a heavenly council

concepts.title: Ugarit and the Canaanite Gods
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1928 a farmer plowing near the Syrian coast broke into an ancient tomb, and excavations from 1929 at the nearby mound of Ras Shamra uncovered the city of Ugarit. Its clay tablets are written in a local alphabetic cuneiform and date mostly from the 13th and early 12th centuries BCE, before the city was destroyed around 1185 BCE. They give the fullest surviving picture of the religion of the wider Canaanite world from which ancient Israel emerged.

At the head of the Ugaritic pantheon sits El, an aged, wise king called "father of years" and "creator of creatures". His consort is Athirat, the goddess the Hebrew Bible calls Asherah. The most active god is Baal, a storm god whose epic, the Baal Cycle, tells how he defeats Yam (Sea) and struggles with Mot (Death). The gods meet as an assembly, the "sons of El" (bn il), with El presiding.

Israel belonged to the same cultural family, even though the Ugaritic texts are centuries older than most of the Bible. The name "Israel" first appears on the Egyptian Merneptah Stele of about 1208 BCE, and most archaeologists now think early Israel grew largely out of the Canaanite population of the central highlands rather than arriving from outside. Its language was a Canaanite dialect, and the name Isra-el is built on El, so Yahweh isn't in it. Open the Bible and you'll find Israel's God given El titles such as El Elyon ("El Most High") and El Shaddai.

concepts.title: A God from the South
concepts.contentHtml:
Yahweh doesn't appear among the gods of Ugarit. Look at the old biblical poems and they have him march from the south: "Yahweh came from Sinai and dawned from Seir" (Deuteronomy 33:2); "when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom" (Judges 5:4); "God came from Teman" (Habakkuk 3:3). Seir and Teman lie in or near Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea. Egyptian lists from Amenhotep III's temple at Soleb (14th century BCE) name a "land of the Shasu of yhw", Shasu being Egypt's word for the region's pastoral nomads. Many scholars see yhw as an early form of the divine name, though it may name a place.

The Kenite (or Midianite) hypothesis, proposed in the 19th century, builds on these clues. In Exodus, Moses meets God while tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, a priest of Midian, and Judges calls Moses' in-laws Kenites. The hypothesis holds that Yahweh worship reached Israel from such southern groups. It's unproven, since the biblical stories were written down late and the Egyptian evidence is thin.

If Yahweh and El were once distinct, they later merged, and Deuteronomy 32:8-9 may preserve a trace. A Dead Sea Scroll (4QDeut-j) says the Most High (Elyon) divided the nations "according to the number of the sons of God", and "Yahweh's portion is his people". The Masoretic Hebrew text reads "sons of Israel"; the Greek Septuagint has "angels of God" or, in some witnesses, "sons of God". Many scholars think the scroll keeps the older reading, picturing the Most High allotting nations to divine sons, with Israel going to Yahweh. Others read the Most High and Yahweh as one god here.

concepts.title: The Divine Council and Yahweh's Asherah
concepts.contentHtml:
The Hebrew Bible keeps traces of the old divine assembly. Look at Psalm 82, which opens "God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment." God then condemns the others for unjust rule, saying "You are gods, children of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, you shall die like mortals." Most critical scholars read this as Israel's God judging the gods of the nations; older Jewish and Christian interpreters often took the "gods" to be human judges or angels. Job 1 and 1 Kings 22 also picture Yahweh enthroned among a heavenly host.

Archaeology adds inscriptions. At Kuntillet Ajrud, a remote way station in northeastern Sinai excavated in 1975 to 1976 and dated to about 800 BCE, writing on large storage jars blesses people "by Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah" and "by Yahweh of Teman and his asherah". A damaged tomb inscription from Khirbet el-Qom, near Hebron, from the later 8th century BCE, appears to bless a man named Uriyahu by Yahweh and "his asherah".

What asherah means here is debated. Some scholars, such as William Dever, see the goddess Asherah as Yahweh's consort. Others note that Hebrew doesn't normally attach "his" to a personal name, so they read a cult object, the wooden pole or stylized tree, also called an asherah, that the Bible repeatedly condemns. Even that symbol was tied to the goddess, and 2 Kings 23 says Josiah removed an image of Asherah from the Jerusalem Temple itself. On any reading, religion in Israel and Judah was less exclusive than the biblical writers wanted.

title: From Many Gods to One
description: Monolatry, royal reforms, exile, and the first explicit monotheism

concepts.title: Monolatry Before Monotheism
concepts.contentHtml:
Historians of religion distinguish monolatry, the worship of one god without denying that other gods exist, from monotheism, the claim that only one god exists at all. (Henotheism is a related term for favoring one god while recognizing others.) Much of the Hebrew Bible reads as monolatry. The first commandment, "you shall have no other gods before me", forbids worshiping other gods rather than denying them. The judge Jephthah tells an enemy king, "Should you not possess what your god Chemosh gives you to possess?" (Judges 11:24), and Micah 4:5 says calmly that "all the peoples walk, each in the name of its god".

Neighboring kingdoms worked the same way. The Mesha Stele of about 840 BCE, a Moabite royal inscription, credits the god Chemosh with Moab's victories over Israel. It also contains the earliest known mention of Yahweh outside the Bible: Mesha boasts of taking objects belonging to Yahweh from the town of Nebo and dragging them before Chemosh. Each people had its national god, and Israel's was Yahweh.

The Bible itself records Israelites worshiping Baal, Asherah, and "the host of heaven". Many scholars, following Morton Smith and Bernhard Lang, describe a "Yahweh-alone" movement: prophets and reformers, such as Elijah in the books of Kings and the prophet Hosea, who insisted that Israel worship Yahweh only. In this reconstruction the movement was a minority voice for a long time. Its view became dominant only over centuries, through royal reforms, national catastrophe, and the editing of the biblical books by people who shared it.

concepts.title: Hezekiah, Josiah, and the Exile
concepts.contentHtml:
The books of Kings credit two kings of Judah with sweeping reforms. Hezekiah (reigned c. 715 to 686 BCE, though some scholars prefer earlier dates) "removed the high places, broke down the pillars, and cut down the sacred pole", and smashed a bronze serpent that tradition traced to Moses (2 Kings 18:4). Archaeologists have pointed to a dismantled horned altar at Beersheba and a decommissioned shrine at Arad as possible evidence, but the dating and meaning of both finds are disputed.

Josiah (reigned c. 640 to 609 BCE) went further. According to 2 Kings 22 to 23, a "book of the law" was found in the Temple in 622 BCE, and Josiah purged the worship of Baal, Asherah, and the heavenly bodies, destroyed rural shrines, and centralized sacrifice in Jerusalem. Since W. M. L. de Wette in 1805, scholars have linked this book to an early form of Deuteronomy, whose laws demand a single sanctuary and exclusive loyalty to Yahweh. How much of the story is history and how much later idealization remains debated; outside evidence is limited.

Then came catastrophe. Babylon took Jerusalem in 597 BCE and destroyed the city and its Temple in 587 or 586 BCE, deporting much of Judah's elite. The Babylonian exile raised an obvious question: whether Yahweh had been defeated by Babylon's gods. The answer that prevailed was the reverse. Yahweh had used Babylon to punish Judah, which implied that he directed the history of every nation. Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BCE and let exiles return; a rebuilt Temple was dedicated around 515 BCE.

concepts.title: No Other God: Second Isaiah and Elephantine
concepts.contentHtml:
Most critical scholars, since the late 18th century, have assigned Isaiah 40 to 55 to a later author than the 8th-century prophet Isaiah of Jerusalem. This anonymous prophet, called Second Isaiah (Deutero-Isaiah), names Cyrus of Persia as Yahweh's "anointed" (Isaiah 45:1), which places him near the end of the exile, around 550 to 539 BCE. Here the Hebrew Bible makes its clearest claim that other gods do not exist: "I am Yahweh, and there is no other; besides me there is no god" (45:5). The prophet mocks the craftsman who carves a god from half a log and cooks his dinner over the other half (44:9 to 20), and makes Yahweh the source of both light and darkness, "weal" and "woe" (45:7).

Some scholars caution that this is the rhetoric of incomparability, aimed at Babylon's gods, rather than abstract philosophy. Still, most see Second Isaiah as the point where Yahweh-alone worship becomes explicit monotheism.

The change did not reach every Jew at once. On Elephantine, an island in the Nile at Aswan, a Jewish military colony served the Persian Empire in the 5th century BCE. Its Aramaic papyri describe a temple of YHW (Yahu), destroyed in 410 BCE and the subject of a petition in 407 BCE to the governor of Judah. Yet a list of contributions records silver collected not only for YHW but also for the deities Eshembethel and Anatbethel, and one oath is sworn by Anat-Yahu, a name joining Yahweh with the goddess Anat.

title: Second Temple Judaism
description: Persian rule, apocalypses, rival sects, and a crowded heaven

concepts.title: Persia and the Zoroastrian Question
concepts.contentHtml:
For two centuries after 539 BCE, Judah was Yehud, a small province of the Persian Empire centered on the rebuilt Temple. Many scholars think the Torah took much of its final shape in this period, though when and how is debated. Persian rule also frames one of the longest arguments in the study of religion: how much Judaism took from Zoroastrianism, the faith associated with Iran.

The case for influence rests on timing. Several ideas that are faint or absent in older Israelite texts grow prominent after contact with Persia: named angels and demons in ranks; a supreme adversary, as "the satan", a prosecutor in God's court in Job and Zechariah, becomes the Devil; a cosmic war of light against darkness, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls; bodily resurrection; and a final judgment followed by a renewed world. Later Zoroastrian texts contain all of these. Hebrew also borrowed the Persian word for an enclosed park, pardes; the same Iranian word, through Greek, gives English "paradise". Scholars such as Mary Boyce and Norman Cohn argued that the borrowing was real and deep.

The case against is mainly about evidence. The Avesta, Zoroastrian scripture, was probably first written down in the Sasanian period, around the 5th or 6th century CE, and the fullest accounts of its end times come from Middle Persian books of the 9th century CE. What Persians believed in 500 BCE is hard to prove. Jewish ideas also have internal roots, such as Ezekiel's vision of dry bones and older Canaanite combat myths. Many scholars now take a middle view: the Persian setting may have encouraged developments that Jewish thought could also generate on its own.

concepts.title: Apocalypses and Sects
concepts.contentHtml:
Alexander the Great took the Levant in 332 BCE. Judea passed to the Ptolemies of Egypt and, around 200 BCE, to the Seleucids of Syria. In 167 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus IV banned Jewish practice and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. The Maccabean revolt won the Temple back, rededicating it in 164 BCE (the origin of Hanukkah).

Persecution fed apocalyptic literature: revelations, often through angels, about heavenly secrets and the coming end of history. Most scholars date the visions of Daniel (chapters 7 to 12) to about 167 to 164 BCE, because they describe Antiochus's actions accurately and then predict a death for him that did not happen as described. Daniel 12:2 is the Hebrew Bible's clearest statement of resurrection: "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." Parts of 1 Enoch, such as the Book of the Watchers about fallen angels, are older, probably 3rd century BCE. 1 Enoch survives complete only in Ge'ez and is scripture in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

The historian Josephus describes three Jewish "philosophies". The Pharisees taught resurrection and an oral tradition alongside the written law; rabbinic Judaism later grew largely from their heirs. The Sadducees, linked to the priestly aristocracy, rejected resurrection. The Essenes kept strict purity rules and shared property. Most scholars identify the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls, found in caves near Qumran from 1947 to 1956, as Essene or closely related, though a minority disputes the link.

concepts.title: A Crowded Heaven: Wisdom, Logos, Son of Man
concepts.contentHtml:
Second Temple Jews worshiped one God and rejected idols, but their heaven was crowded. Beside the angels stood exalted figures who acted for God, and they matter for what came next. Some scholars doubt that "monotheism", a word coined in the 17th century, fits ancient Judaism at all; others keep it, provided it means exclusive worship rather than an empty heaven.

Wisdom is personified in Proverbs 8, where she says she was set up "at the first, before the beginning of the earth" and was beside God at creation "like a master worker". Ben Sira, writing around 180 BCE, identifies Wisdom with the Torah; the Wisdom of Solomon calls her "a breath of the power of God". The Alexandrian Jewish philosopher Philo (c. 20 BCE to c. 50 CE) joined this to Greek philosophy in his teaching on the Logos, God's Word or Reason, the instrument through which God made the world. Philo called the Logos God's "firstborn" and once even a "second god", while insisting that God is one.

The Son of Man begins in Daniel 7:13, where "one like a son of man", a human-like figure, comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. Scholars debate whether he is an angel such as Michael or a symbol of faithful Israel. In the Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 37 to 71, probably 1st century BCE or 1st century CE), the Son of Man is a preexistent heavenly judge seated on a throne of glory. Later rabbis condemned belief in "two powers in heaven", which suggests that some people, perhaps Jews as well as Christians, held something like it.

title: The First Christians
description: A Jewish sect, early devotion to Jesus, rival Christianities, and the Trinity

concepts.title: A Jewish Messianic Movement
concepts.contentHtml:
Jesus of Nazareth was a Jew from Galilee, executed by the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate around 30 CE. His first followers were Jews who believed God had raised him from the dead and that he was the Messiah. They kept worshiping at the Temple; the Jerusalem community was led by Peter and later by James, the brother of Jesus, whom Josephus says was executed in 62 CE. Acts calls them "the sect of the Nazarenes". Christianity began inside Second Temple Judaism, which by then firmly worshiped one God.

The earliest Christian writings are the letters of Paul, a former Pharisee who wrote between about 50 and 60 CE. Nearly all scholars accept seven letters as his: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Paul argued that non-Jews could join God's people through faith in Christ without circumcision or the full Jewish law, which opened the movement to the wider Roman world.

The separation of Christianity from Judaism, called the parting of the ways, was a long, uneven process rather than one break. The older idea that a rabbinic council at Yavneh around 90 CE expelled Christians is now widely doubted. As late as 386 to 387 CE, John Chrysostom preached sermons in Antioch attacking Christians who still attended synagogue and kept Jewish festivals. Scholars such as Daniel Boyarin argue that the boundary was drawn slowly, by authorities on both sides.

concepts.title: Devotion to Jesus: Early or Gradual?
concepts.contentHtml:
Paul's letters, written 20 to 30 years after Jesus' death, already show devotion to him. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul writes of "one God, the Father, from whom are all things" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things", wording that seems to divide the Shema, Judaism's confession of one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), between the Father and Jesus. Philippians 2:10 to 11 applies to Jesus a verse in which Yahweh says "to me every knee shall bow" (Isaiah 45:23), from Second Isaiah's most monotheistic chapter. The Aramaic prayer maranatha, "our Lord, come!" (1 Corinthians 16:22), suggests Aramaic-speaking believers already called on Jesus in prayer.

Scholars of early high Christology, notably Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham, argue that this devotion arose within the first two decades among Jewish believers. Hurtado called it a "mutation" in Jewish monotheism and stressed practice: prayer, hymns, baptism, and meals in Jesus' name. Bauckham argued that Jesus was included in the unique identity of Israel's one God from the start.

Scholars favoring gradual development, among them Bart Ehrman, James Dunn, and Maurice Casey, each in a different way, read the same texts more cautiously. Ehrman argues that the earliest believers saw Jesus as a man exalted to divine status at his resurrection, citing Romans 1:3 to 4 ("declared to be Son of God with power... by resurrection from the dead"). He accepts that Paul already thought of Christ as a preexistent heavenly being, but sees a long development. Both sides agree that by the Gospel of John, around 90 to 110 CE, Jesus could be called God: "the Word was God".

concepts.title: Many Christianities and the Trinity
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 2nd century, groups calling themselves Christian disagreed deeply about God. The Ebionites, described by Irenaeus around 180 CE, were Jewish believers who kept the Torah, rejected Paul, and saw Jesus as a human Messiah. Marcion of Sinope, who broke with the church in Rome around 144 CE, taught two gods: the just but harsh creator of the Hebrew Bible, and a higher, wholly good Father revealed by Jesus. His scripture, an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul, is the earliest known Christian canon. Gnostic teachers described a heavenly fullness (pleroma) of emanations called aeons, and an ignorant lesser creator, the demiurge, named Yaldabaoth in the Apocryphon of John, who boasts that there is no other god. Many such texts were found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945.

Mainstream Christians rejected these views but still had to explain how Father, Son, and Spirit relate within one God. Tertullian used the Latin trinitas in the early 3rd century. In Alexandria the priest Arius (c. 256 to 336) taught that the Son was created by the Father before time: "there was when he was not". The Council of Nicaea (325), called by Constantine, declared the Son homoousios, "of the same substance" as the Father, "begotten, not made". Argument went on for decades. The Council of Constantinople (381) affirmed the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, completing the classic doctrine of one God in three persons, which Christians understand as monotheism, not three gods.

title: Islam's Setting
description: Arabia's gods, its Jews and Christians, and how historians study early Islam

concepts.title: Gods of Pre-Islamic Arabia
concepts.contentHtml:
Islamic tradition calls the time before Islam the jahiliyya, "the age of ignorance". The evidence for its religion is uneven: the Quran itself, later Muslim writers such as Hisham ibn al-Kalbi (died c. 820), whose Book of Idols catalogs shrines, and thousands of pre-Islamic inscriptions.

The Quran portrays the Meccans it addresses as already acknowledging Allah as creator: "If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say 'Allah'" (29:61). Their fault, in its terms, was shirk, associating other beings with God; they say of their deities, "we only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah" (39:3). The name Allah is usually explained as a contraction of al-ilah, "the god", related to Hebrew El and Aramaic Alaha. Muhammad's father, by tradition, was named Abd Allah, "servant of God".

Three goddesses are named together in Quran 53:19 to 20: al-Lat, with a shrine at Ta'if; al-Uzza, "the mighty one", worshiped at Nakhla near Mecca; and Manat, a goddess of fate, with a shrine at Qudayd near the coast. Some Arabs called them daughters of Allah, which the Quran rejects. The Kaaba in Mecca, which the Quran says Abraham and Ishmael raised (2:127), stood in a sacred zone where fighting was forbidden; tradition says it held an image of the god Hubal among many idols, which Muhammad removed in 630 CE. Tradition also names a few hanifs, seekers of Abraham's pure monotheism before Islam, such as Zayd ibn Amr, though historians debate how far these reports reflect later memory.

concepts.title: Jews and Christians in Arabia
concepts.contentHtml:
Arabia was not cut off from the monotheisms of the Near East. In the southwest, the kingdom of Himyar, in today's Yemen, changed sharply around 380 CE: royal inscriptions stop naming the old gods and invoke one God, called Rahmanan, "the Merciful", and "Lord of heaven and earth". Most scholars, following the epigrapher Christian Robin, conclude that Himyar's ruling elite adopted a form of Judaism, though how far the wider population followed is unclear.

The story turned violent in the 6th century. The Himyarite king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, called Dhu Nuwas in Islamic sources, persecuted the Christians of Najran around 523 CE. The Christian kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia, whose king Ezana had adopted Christianity in the 4th century, invaded around 525 and ended Jewish rule. The Aksumite general Abraha then made himself ruler of Yemen. Islamic tradition tells of Abraha marching on Mecca with an elephant in the "Year of the Elephant", traditionally the year of Muhammad's birth, c. 570. Abraha's own inscriptions record a campaign into central Arabia in 552, and historians debate how the two relate.

To the north, the Ghassanids, Arab allies of the Byzantine Empire, were Christians, and the Lakhmid capital of al-Hira, allied with Persia, had a strong Christian community of the Church of the East. In Yathrib, later Medina, Jewish tribes such as the Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, and Banu Qurayza lived beside Arab clans. Biblical figures and stories were part of Arabia's religious conversation long before Islam.

concepts.title: Muhammad's Mission and the Historians
concepts.contentHtml:
According to Muslim sources, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE into the Quraysh tribe and began receiving revelations around 610. Muslims believe the Quran is the word of God revealed to him. Its central message is tawhid, the oneness of God, and it presents itself as confirming earlier revelation to Moses and Jesus and restoring the religion of Abraham, "neither a Jew nor a Christian, but a hanif" (3:67). Muhammad moved to Yathrib in 622 (the hijra, year 1 of the Islamic calendar), took Mecca in 630, and died in 632. Historians note how directly the Quran addresses this setting: polytheists, Jews, and Christians.

The detailed biography comes from later writers, chiefly Ibn Ishaq (died c. 767), known through Ibn Hisham's edition. In the 1970s revisionists challenged the traditional account: John Wansbrough argued that the Quran took shape over two centuries, and Patricia Crone and Michael Cook, in Hagarism (1977), tried to rebuild early Islam from non-Muslim sources alone.

Physical evidence has since narrowed the debate. In 2015 two parchment leaves at the University of Birmingham, containing parts of suras 18 to 20, were radiocarbon-dated to 568 to 645 CE at 95.4% probability. Radiocarbon dates the animal skin, not the writing, but the result fits a written Quran by the mid-7th century. Most scholars now reject very late dates for the Quran, while debating its earliest history. Non-Muslim sources also mention Muhammad early: a Syriac chronicle of about 640 records a battle in 634 involving "the Arabs of Muhammad". Fred Donner has argued that the first community called itself "Believers" and may have included some Jews and Christians.

title: Roots in South Asia and Iran
description: Vedic gods, the Indo-Iranian split, Zoroaster, and the sramana movements

concepts.title: From Indra to Vishnu and Shiva
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest Indian scripture, the Rigveda, is a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, composed in the northwest of the subcontinent roughly between 1500 and 1000 BCE and passed down orally for many centuries before it was written. Its religion centers on yajna, sacrifice offered into fire. Indra, the warrior storm god who kills the serpent Vritra and releases the waters, receives about a quarter of the hymns. Agni, fire itself, carries offerings to the gods and is second in praise. Soma, at once a plant, the drink pressed from it, and a god, fills the entire ninth book; which plant it was is still debated.

Two later great gods are minor here. Vishnu has only a handful of hymns, praising his three strides across the universe. Rudra, a fierce god of disease and healing, has only a few; shiva, "auspicious", is at first an epithet. Over the next thousand years, as the Upanishads, epics, and Puranas took shape, Vishnu and Shiva rose to supremacy. Devotion (bhakti) to a personal god grew, and Vishnu absorbed other figures as his avatars, among them Krishna and Rama. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, set up around 113 BCE by a Greek envoy, honors Vasudeva (Krishna) as "god of gods".

Indra survived as king of the lesser gods but shrank in stature. A Puranic story makes the point: when Indra sends a storm on cowherds who stopped his worship at Krishna's urging, Krishna lifts Mount Govardhana like an umbrella and Indra yields. Hinduism, a modern umbrella term, grew from these layers rather than from one founder.

concepts.title: Devas and Ahuras: The Indo-Iranian Split
concepts.contentHtml:
Vedic Sanskrit and Avestan, the language of Zoroastrian scripture, are close enough that some lines can be converted from one to the other by regular sound rules. They descend from a shared Indo-Iranian heritage, and so do many religious terms: Vedic soma and Avestan haoma, Vedic Mitra and Avestan Mithra, Vedic rta and Avestan asha (cosmic truth and order). A 14th-century BCE treaty between the Hittites and the kingdom of Mitanni in northern Syria even invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatyas.

Then the vocabularies diverge. In the Rigveda the gods are devas, and asura is at first an honorable title, applied especially to Varuna; in later Vedic texts the asuras become demonic enemies of the devas. In Iran the reverse happened: the supreme god is Ahura Mazda, the "Wise Lord", while the daevas are false gods or demons, and a later Avestan text lists Indra among them. Some 19th-century scholars saw the trace of a religious schism here; many now think both shifts were gradual.

The reformer on the Iranian side was Zarathustra (Greek Zoroaster), traditionally the author of the Gathas, 17 hymns in archaic Old Avestan. His dates are unresolved. Zoroastrian tradition puts him "258 years before Alexander", in the 6th century BCE, but many scholars see that as a late calculation. Because Gathic Avestan is so close to Rigvedic Sanskrit, many place him far earlier, roughly 1500 to 1000 BCE (Mary Boyce argued for c. 1400 to 1000), while others still defend a 7th- or 6th-century date. Around 520 BCE the Persian king Darius I credited his rule to Ahuramazda in the Behistun inscription, though whether the early Persian kings were Zoroastrians is itself debated.

concepts.title: The Sramanas: Buddhism and Jainism
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 5th century BCE the Ganges plain was changing fast, with new cities, trade, coinage, and kingdoms such as Magadha and Kosala. In this world appeared the sramanas (shramana, "striver"), wandering renouncers who left household life and rejected the authority of the Vedas and the brahmin priests' sacrifices. They argued with one another: the Ajivikas held that fate determines everything, while materialists denied rebirth altogether. Many shared ideas also found in the early Upanishads: karma, rebirth (samsara), and liberation through discipline and insight. Whether these ideas began among brahmins or in a non-Vedic culture of the east, as Johannes Bronkhorst has argued, is debated.

Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born into the Shakya clan at Lumbini, a site the emperor Ashoka marked with an inscribed pillar in the 3rd century BCE. Older books date his death to c. 483 BCE; most historians now place it around 400 BCE. He taught a middle way between indulgence and harsh asceticism, leading to the end of suffering in nirvana. Buddhism did not deny the Vedic gods; it demoted them. In the texts Brahma and Indra are powerful but mortal beings, still caught in rebirth, and Brahma himself begs the Buddha to teach.

Mahavira, an older contemporary of the Buddha, is for Jains the 24th tirthankara ("ford-maker") of the present age, following Parshva, who may also have been historical. Jainism teaches that karma is a fine matter clinging to the soul, removed through strict nonviolence (ahimsa) and austerity. Like Buddhism, it has no creator god. Hinduism later absorbed many sramana ideals, such as renunciation and nonviolence.
